text: Explain, in detail, the Vision of AG Lafely. Explain the model as postulated by Lafely for P&G. Cite company’s product as examples in each case. Vig OPEN INNOVATION: THE CASE OF P&G By Taranjeet Chawla, IBS Research Centre, Kolkata ‘We want P&G to be known as the company that collaborates — inside and out — better than any other company in the world.” -A G Lafley, president and CEO, P&G “P&G has a history of acquiring technologies from outside our Company. What is particularly new in our Connect + Develop approach to external relationships is our strong focus on ready-to-go innovations.” -Gil Cloyd, CTO, P&G “Today, P&G is the model of open innovation implemented effectively, and their financial results demonstrate the power of the approach.” -Michael Docherty, CEO of Venture2 Inc." INTRODUCTION - By 2000, Procter & Gamble (P&G), one of the world’s largest consumer products companies, was under immense pressure. For decades, the company was known for its innovation. The consistent growth of the company was largely driven by innovation from within the organization, relying heavily on in-house R&D. For a long time, this centralized innovation model worked well for P&G. However, by 2000, it realized that an internally focused model of innovatiori was not sustainable as the success rate of new products (developed independently by the R&D department) was around 35%. Besides, the R&D expenses were escalating faster, increasing by $500 million between 1996 and 2000 to reach $1,899 million. By mid 2000, the company’s share prices fell by more than 50%. Worried by the situation, the company's newly appointed CEO, Alan G Lafley (Lafley) decided to reinvent P&G’s innovation model. He felt that outside connections could discover new ideas from around the world which could quickly be turned into innovative products by using the company’s own R&D, manufacturing and marketing skills. Thus le ‘began to focus on external collaborations to bring in innovative ideas and then applied internal capabilities to develop new products. This model was termed as ‘connect and develop’ (C&D) innovation model. He believed that the new model would enable the company slash its R&D costs and increase the success rate of new ' Michael Docherty is the CEO of Venture2 Inc., a consulting and new ventures management company focused on launching breakthrough innovation in the consumer products industry. *"e innovations. He set a goal to create 50% of the innovations outside the company’s R&D labs. The new innovation model proved to be fruitful for P&G and it introduced several successful products using the model. Experts opined that companies which would not adopt this model would find it difficult to survive. P&G: AT A GLANCE P&G was established on October 31°, 1837 when William Procter, a candle-maker, and James Gamble, a soap-maker, formed business partnership in Cincinnati, Ohio (US) Initially, the company concentrated on manufacturing and marketing of both, soaps and candles, reaching $1 million in sales by 1859. Later, it began to focus more on soap and had a range of more than 30 different types of soap by the 1890s. In the early 19” century, the company’ began to diversify its products and introduced Crisco”, a shortening made from vegetable oils rather than animal fat, in 1911. In the wake of growing popularity of electric bulbs, it stopped manufacturing candles in 1920. During this time, the company started hiring researchers for conducting research in various fields (especially chemical) and developing new products. The research efforts of the company led to the introduction of Dreft, the first synthetic detergent powder, in 1933 and Drene, the first detergent-based shampoo, in 1934. Drene also marked P&G's entry into the hair care business. Later, in 1946, it launched Tide, laundry detergent, and Prell a shampoo brand. In 1952, the company opened Miami Valley Laboratories (MVL) in Cincinnati, which was its first facility solely dedicated to research. In 1955, the company launched Crest, the first toothpaste to use fluoride as an ingredient. Crest was approved by the American Dental Association (ADA) as an ‘effective decay-preventive dentifrice that can be of significant value’*®. Over a period of time, the crest brand was associated with about 20 different products (such as toothbrushes, toothpaste, mouthwash, dental floss and tooth-whitening products). In 1960, P&G launched liquid Downy, its first fabric softener, and a year later, it test ‘ prt Pampers, a brand of disposable diapers. Pampers was the result of the télentless R&D efforts put in by the researchers of the company to design a diaper that ? Crisco was the first all-vegetable shortening. Crisco provided a healthier alternative to cooking with animal fats and was more economical than butter. ‘Crest toothpaste’, http: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Crest_toothpaste was absorbent, disposable and prevented leaks. Prior to the launch of Pampers disposable diapers were not popular. However, Pampers was an instant hit with customers and replaced cloth diapers. Launched in 1972, Bouhce, fabric softener sheets, was another example of innovative product, which was used to soften clothes in the dryer. In 1983, P&G introduced Always/Whisper, a feminine protection product which, by 1985 became one of the world’s leading brands in its category. It launched Pert Plus/Rejoice shampoo in 1986 which enabled consumers to wash and condition their hair using just one product: Apart from innoavtive products, P&G innovated its packaging also. In Germany, it introduced refill packs for liquid products, such as Lenor fabric softener. it was viewed as a major step towards solid waste prevention and. was named ‘the invention of the year’ by German grocers. In 1990, it won the ‘International DuPont Packaging Award’ for its Spic and Span Pine*, a house-hold cleanser, which was packaged in 100% recycled plastic. P&G was also awarded the ‘National Medal of Technology’* for creating, developing and applying advanced technologies to consumer _ products. In 1996, P&G developed a new product, Olestra, which was a calorie-free substitue for fat in cooking potato chips and other snacks. Olestra, marketed under the brand name of Olean, got the approval of the FDA® to be used in salty snack and crackers. In 2000, the company received FDA's approval for its new product, Actonel (risedronate sodium tablets) for the treatment of postmenopausal osteoporosis (PMO) “and glucocorticoid- induced osteoporosis (GIO) At the end of 2000, P&G had a global network of 18 technical centers in 9 countries spread across 4 continents. It had more than 8,000 scientists and researchers working in its Jabs on new product development. By the end of financial year 2000, ten of P&G's brands generated over.a billion dollar each in sales annually. These included Pampers yl & 50 January 2001, P&G sold Spic and Span to Shansby Group, a San Francisco investment firm. 5 The National Medal of Technology is an honor granted by the President of the United States to inventors and innovators (a person, a group of people or an organization) that have made significant contributions to the development of new and important technology. It is the highest honor in the US for achievements related to technological progress. ® The Food and Drug Administration is an agency of the United States Department of Health and Human Services and is responsible for regulating food, dietary supplements, drugs, cosmetics, etc. in the US. 4/12 Tide, Ariel, Pantene, Bounty, Charmin, Always, Folgers, Downy and Pringles. The company ended the year with sales worth $40 billion up 5% from 1999. However, net earnings were down 6% to $3.5 billion from $3.7 billion in the previous year [Exhibit FROM R&D TO C&D: A NEW APPROACH TO INNOVATION ’We're probably as good as the next guy at inventing. But we are not absolutely and positively better than everybody else at inventing. There are a lot of good inventors out there.” -AG Lafley, CEO, P&G In 2000, P&G invested almost $1.9 billion or 4.75% of sales in R&D [Exhibit 2] for developing new products. This brought the company to the list of 20 largest R&D investors which included Pfizer, General Electric, Sony, Merck, Hewlett-Packard, etc. However, the success rate of its new products was around 35%. Triggered by virtually flat sales and a fall in earnings, the net earnings margin dropped to 8.9% from 9.9% in 1999. As a result, P&G's share price slid from $118 to $52 a share. In 2001, the company’s earnings further declined to $2.6 billion and the margin shrank to 6.7%. Amidst the difficult times, CEO Lafley, who took over after Durk |. Jager (Durk) resigned in June 2000, faced the challenge of reorganizing the company’s innovation model. While his predecessor Durk tried to invent more new products internally by ) revamping the R&D department, Lafley had a different vision [Exhibit 3]. He wanted around half of the innovation ideas to come from outside. He expressed, “My hypothesis is that innovation and discovery are likely to come from anywhere. What P&G is really good at is developing innovations and commercializing them. So what   said is, ‘We ” need an open marketplace. Traditionally, most of P&G’s innovations were created in its own R&D labs by connecting ideas/internally within the organization. However, observing a few products, which had used, pre ideas taken from outside, proved that external collaborations too could produce highly successful innovations. With this concept in mind, Lafley created C&D innovations model [Exhibit 4]. The basic principle of the model was that promising ideas were available throughout the globe and by using them the company could create 5A superior and cheaper products, faster. P&G’s connect and develop was often mistaken to be simply outsourcing which meant transferring work to low-cost providers. However the company clearly differentiated its C&D from outsourcing, emphasizing that it was about identifying innovative ideas from outside and bringing them into the organization to capitalize on its own R&D capabilities. In order for C&D to work, the company first identified what it was looking for and then decided to look for ideas that were already in use somewhere. After the idea was identified the company then focused on those ideas . and products that could be turned into successful product using its own R&D capabilities. For searching. ideas the company discovered three different sources: to identify top the consumer needs, adjacencies, and technology game boards. IDENTIFYING TOP TEN CONSUMER NEEDS For all its businesses, P&G, once a year, prepared a list of top ten consumer needs which, when satisfied, would boost the growth of their brands. Based on these lists another list for the company overall was prepared and then the needs were developed into problems to be solved. These problems were clearly detailed in technology briefs solutions to which were to be found outside the company. FINDING ADJACENCIES The company also attempted to find how new products or concept could benefit from existing brand equity. In this exercise the company identified products that were adjacent to its existing products and then sought relevant innovation in those product categories. TECHNOLOGY GAME BOARDS Another source of idea search was technology game boards which helped assess the impact of technology acquisition in one area on the products in other categories. These game boards explored various questions, such as which technologies the company wanted to strengthen, which technologies it wanted to acquire or which of them it wanted ta sell out. Answers to these questions provided broad targets for innovation searches. Once the company ‘decided what ideas to look for and identified the sources of ideas, it needed a global network to carry out the activities that formed the C&D model. P&G's own network across the globe provided a platform for the application of C&D strategies. It used closed proprietary networks and open networks for the purpose. Closed 6 /ig proprietary networks comprised of technology entrepreneurs, suppliers etc. while open networks included individuals, organizations, educational and research institutions government and private labs, competitors, trade partners, etc. P&G developed various closed proprietary networks for undertaking C&D activities. The most important of them were technology entrepreneurs and: suppliers. Technology entrepreneurs were senior P&G managers who were responsible for preparing technology briefs, defining the problem to be solved. They established external connections (such as liaisoning with researchers, forming supplier networks, etc.) and communicated.those connections to the company’s business unit heads. The technology entrepreneurs combined scientific literature and patent databases with physical hunt for ideas since searching ideas electronically alone was not sufficient. A technology entrepreneur in Japan, while exploring the market, found a product that was eventually developed and sold as ‘Mr. Clean Magic Eraser’ [Exhibit 5]. The company had a network of 70 technology entrepreneurs who worked out of six C&D hubs in the US Latin America, Western Europe, Japan, China and India. All the hubs focused on finding products, concepts or technologies that were the specialties of their respective regions. By early 2006, technology entrepreneurs had identified around 10,000 products, ideas and technologies. The supplier base of the company formed another network for C&D activities. The top 15 suppliers to the company had a combined R&D staff of approximately 50,000. VWhen the company began to embrace C&D model it realized that the huge researcher base of its suppliers could be a potential source of innovation. Subsequently, P&G developed a highly secure IT platform that enabled it to share its problems (technology briefs) with its suppliers. The company even went to the extent of sending its researchers to suppliers’ labs to work with theirs and inviting suppliers’ researchers to: work with its own. According to Larry Huston, vice president, innovation and knowledge, P&G, said, “In some cases, suppliers’ researchers come to work in our labs, an in.others, we work in thelrs — an example of what we call ‘cocreation’, a type of collaboration that goes well yond typical joint development.” The company also held meetings with suppliers ca its top managers interacted with suppliers’ top leaders understanding each other's capabilities. Ag To complement the closed proprietary networks, the company used open networks. Examples of open network, which were very useful for the company, were: NineSigma InnoCentive, YourEncore and Yet2.com. NineSigma: P&G was instrumental in creating NineSigma, a firm that connected companies that had problems with those companies, universities, academic institutions government and private research labs that could find solutions to those problems. NineSigma prepared a technology brief that described a problem and distributed it to its network of solution providers. In case someone had a solution to the problem, the message was conveyed to the company (that had the problem). If the company found the solution to be relevant to its requirement, NineSigma connected the solution provider with the company and the research project started.
